approachQuestion.prompt:
First alarm. A read-only array levels contains n arbitrary signed integer readings in chronological order. Return the smallest index whose reading is strictly positive, or -1 if none is positive. There are 1 <= n <= 200,000 readings; each fits one fixed-size word. Readings have no ordering or monotonicity guarantee. Choose minimum worst-case time, then peak auxiliary storage. Indexed reads and comparisons cost constant time; return only one index.

Example 1: Input: levels=[0,-3,8,-1,5]. Output: 2.
Example 2: Input: levels=[0,-2,0]. Output: -1.

options.text: Scan from index zero, return immediately on the first positive reading, and return -1 if the scan finishes.
options.feedback: The first positive encountered in index order is the earliest alarm. Stopping there is safe because no later reading can improve that index.

options.text: Build a full boolean array recording which readings are positive, then scan its flags from index zero for the first true value.
options.feedback: It returns the correct earliest index for every input, but the flag copy is unnecessary and prevents stopping while reading the original array.

options.text: Check a midpoint; if it is positive search only the left half, otherwise search only the right half.
options.feedback: A nonpositive midpoint does not exclude an earlier positive. For [7,0,0], midpoint index 1 is zero, so this discards the required answer at index 0.

options.text: Scan all readings and overwrite the answer with every positive index.
options.feedback: This returns the last alarm. For [2,3], it returns 1 instead of the earliest index 0.

feedback.reason: An early return improves favorable executions but does not remove inputs that require a complete scan.
details: Start at index zero and inspect readings in order. Return the current index as soon as its value is positive. If every entry is nonpositive, return -1. Retain no flags or candidate list.

A positive first entry permits immediate success, but an all-nonpositive array forces a complete scan before returning -1. Arbitrary chronological values provide no monotone predicate for binary search. State the worst-case bound separately from the best case of early termination.

“Scan from index zero, return immediately on the first positive reading, and return -1 if the scan finishes.”: The first positive encountered in index order is the earliest alarm. Stopping there is safe because no later reading can improve that index.

“Build a full boolean array recording which readings are positive, then scan its flags from index zero for the first true value.”: It returns the correct earliest index for every input, but the flag copy is unnecessary and prevents stopping while reading the original array.

“Check a midpoint; if it is positive search only the left half, otherwise search only the right half.”: A nonpositive midpoint does not exclude an earlier positive. For [7,0,0], midpoint index 1 is zero, so this discards the required answer at index 0.
“Scan all readings and overwrite the answer with every positive index.”: This returns the last alarm. For [2,3], it returns 1 instead of the earliest index 0.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For scan-until-alarm, choose worst-case time and peak auxiliary space as functions of n. A positive reading may occur at the first position, last position, or nowhere. Analyze the worst legal input, not only the quickest early return. No recursion or hashing is used.
constraints: Choose the tightest standard bound for the complete execution. Count peak simultaneously live auxiliary storage; exclude supplied input and required output.
Word arithmetic, indexing, and copying one fixed-size element take constant time. No hashing or recursion is used.

feedback.reason: A no-alarm input forces n tests; early success only changes the best case.
details: An array with no positive reading forces all n entries to be inspected. The method therefore has tight worst-case O(n) time, even though a first-position alarm gives constant best-case work. Only an index and the current word are retained, so auxiliary space is O(1); no copied flag array exists.
“O(1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: An early return gives a fast best case. An absent or last-position alarm still takes n reads.
“O(log(n + 1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The arbitrary readings do not permit discarding half the search space after a comparison.
“O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: The analyzed method reads the input directly and does not allocate boolean flags.
